cards.text: The writer of Hebrews has just walked through a long list of people who lived by faith: Abraham, Moses, Rahab and many more. Now he turns to his readers and says we're surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses. Friend, that is a LOT of company.

cards.question: With that great cloud of witnesses all around, what does the writer tell his readers to do?

answers.text: Run with endurance the race set out for them
Sit back and watch the faithful go first
Build a monument to remember the faithful

cards.text: Nobody wins a race wearing three coats with a cookie box under each arm. So the writer says to throw off every encumbrance, all of it, OFF.

cards.question: Along with every encumbrance, what else does the writer say to throw off before the race?

answers.text: The sin that so easily entangles
The friends who hold them back
The worries that keep them awake

cards.question: Every runner needs somewhere to look. The writer says: let us fix our eyes on ___.

cards.text: The writer calls Jesus the author and perfecter of our faith. And Jesus ran His own race all the way: He endured the cross.

cards.question: Jesus endured the cross. What does the writer say was set before Him?
The writer says Jesus endured the cross, scorning its shame.
Jesus finished the race of the cross. Where does the writer say He sat down?

answers.text: At the right hand of the throne of God
Beside Moses on the holy mountain

cards.text: Then the writer says to consider Him, the One who endured such hostility from sinners. Not glance at Him while scrolling, friend. CONSIDER Him.

cards.question: Consider Jesus, who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow ___ and lose heart.

cards.text: Then the writer turns to his readers and their own struggle against sin. This is the coach leaning on the fence after your laps, and you KNOW he's about to say something.

cards.question: The writer says his readers have already resisted sin to the point of shedding their blood.

cards.text: Then the writer says his readers have forgotten an exhortation that speaks right to them. Forgot it, like me hunting all over the bakery for my timer while it's ringing in my own mustache.

cards.question: That exhortation speaks to a son about the discipline of the Lord. How should he take it?
According to that exhortation, why does the Lord discipline someone?

answers.text: Because they owe Him a debt

cards.text: Endure suffering as discipline, the writer says. God is treating you as sons.

cards.question: The writer asks: what son is not disciplined by his ___?
The writer says a child who never experiences discipline is a true son.

cards.text: We all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. And as a dad myself, I can tell you nobody enjoys the dad talk, not the kid, not the dad, NOBODY.

cards.question: We respected the earthly fathers who disciplined us. What does the writer say we should do with the Father of our spirits?

answers.text: Submit to Him much more and live
Respect Him about the same amount
Keep a careful distance from Him

cards.text: Our earthly fathers disciplined us for a short time, as they thought best. Bless them, they were baking from scratch with no recipe.

cards.question: But God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His ___.

cards.text: The writer is honest: no discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Ask the dough during kneading, friend, push, fold, PUNCH, and that dough is NOT having a good day.

cards.question: Later on, discipline yields a harvest of righteousness and ___ to those who have been trained by it.

cards.text: Then the writer heads back to the race with one more Therefore. Picture the last lap: hands hanging limp, knees wobbling like a stack of cookie boxes on a bumpy road.

cards.question: Hands are limp and knees are weak. What does the writer say to do with them?
The writer says to make straight paths for your feet so that the lame may be healed and not disabled.

findings.problem: The card tells Hebrews 11's long list of people who lived by faith and names Abraham, who first appears at Hebrews 11:8. The list itself starts with Abel at 11:4. The citation starts at Hebrews 11:17, which is narrower than what the card tells.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'The sin that so easily entangles', is the only answer in Bible wording. The wrong answers ('The friends who hold them back', 'The worries that keep them awake') sound modern, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: 'Jesus ran His own race all the way' states as fact a link the text never makes. Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross. It does not call this His race.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question says 'Jesus finished the race of the cross.' Hebrews 12:2 never calls the cross a race. That link between Jesus and the readers' race is stated as fact.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The second half of Hebrews 12:5, 'do not lose heart when He rebukes you', is never told or asked anywhere in the walkthrough. It is a key part of the exhortation, and it echoes 'lose heart' in 12:3.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin says 'We all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them' in his own voice, without saying it's the writer speaking. That claims Papa Dorin had an earthly father who disciplined him, which adds to his backstory.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin says 'Our earthly fathers disciplined us' in his own voice, without saying it's the writer speaking. That claims Papa Dorin had an earthly father, which adds to his backstory.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: 'The writer heads back to the race' states as fact that Hebrews 12:12 returns to the race picture. Verses 12 and 13 talk about hands, knees and paths but never mention a race, so the link is the text's to leave open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.
